Gas-powered and rechargeable battery generators have long been go-to options for home backup power and on-location electricity. However, advances in solar technology have made solar-powered portable generators a genuinely compelling, emissions-free alternative for a wide range of users — from full-time off-gridders to occasional campers.

In this guide, we compare five of the best solar portable generators on the market today. You'll find a head-to-head specs comparison, in-depth reviews of each model, and a practical buying guide to help you match a generator to your specific needs and budget.

How we chose the best solar portable generators

By weighting these factors, we selected five models that represent the strongest options for off-grid living, emergency backup power, and recreational use.

Real-world outage scenarios: what the data shows

PowerOutage.us has tracked every major U.S. outage event since 2016, and that continuous monitoring informs how we think about solar generator capacity requirements. The following examples from our event database illustrate why sizing your solar generator correctly matters so much.

Winter Storm Fern

During Winter Storm Fern (January 2026), over one million customers lost power at the storm’s peak, with Tennessee bearing the brunt at 306,700 customers. Many were in the Nashville metro. The hardest-hit households went six or more days without electricity as ice snapped trees and overwhelmed repair crews. The storm's 2,000-mile area stretched from New Mexico to New England, underscoring that winter outages can be a nationwide concern.

Hurricane Helene

Hurricane Helene (September 2024) remains the largest event PowerOutage.us tracked in 2024, with 4.79 million customers affected. Western North Carolina's mountain communities faced outages exceeding 14 days. This was a scenario where a mid-size 2,000 Wh station would have been exhausted within two days of moderate use, and only a high-capacity unit with solar recharging could sustain emergency household energy through the full duration.

Hurricane Milton

Hurricane Milton (October 2024) revealed a different challenge: cycling grid failures, with power coming on and off for brief windows of 30 minutes to two hours. That pattern put a premium on fast-charging solar generators that could top off batteries during those windows. For example, the advantages that units like the Goal Zero Yeti PRO 4000 and EcoFlow DELTA Pro 3 hold over slower-charging alternatives.

Overall, these events show households can make use of solar generators with enough capacity to last multiple days and enough solar input to keep recharging without relying on the grid.

Benefits of solar generators vs. gas generators

Solar portable generators have a number of distinct advantages for partial home backup and recreational use. Some notable benefits include:

Clean, renewable energy source with zero emissions
Free energy generation from solar power
No need to store flammable, unstable fuel
Fewer maintenance needs than combustible engine generators
Safer to operate as an emergency backup energy source in homes
Can also be charged from grid power through your home electrical system
Silent operation for annoyance-free nighttime or indoor use

Note that while solar portable generators are safer to use in homes due to the absence of emissions and combustible fuel, it is still important to follow basic generator safety precautions. Refer to your solar generator's user manual for safe operating guidelines. Whole-home backup claims also assume load management, compatible transfer equipment, and in many cases multiple battery units.

Note that a solar generator doesn't technically generate electricity, it stores it. You charge it either by connecting solar panels or plugging into a wall outlet, then draw on that stored energy when you need it. Without a recharge source, a fully depleted unit simply won't power anything until it's recharged.

What to look for in a solar portable generator

Solar generators come with long lists of technical specifications, but some are more relevant for usability than others. Here are the key features worth focusing on.

Battery specifications
Type: Lithium-ion batteries have become the industry standard over traditional lead-acid deep-cycle batteries, due to their superior capacity and faster charging. LFP (LiFePO₄) chemistry offers particularly strong cycle life and is used by several units on our list.
Capacity: Typically measured in watt-hours or kilowatt-hours, capacity represents the maximum amount of energy a battery can hold in reserve.
Cycle life: The total number of times a battery can be fully depleted and recharged before capacity degrades meaningfully.
Inverter type

Pure sine wave inverters are more efficient than modified sine wave alternatives and produce cleaner electrical current that's safe for sensitive electronics like laptops, CPAP machines, and medical devices. Most solar generators on our list feature pure sine wave inverters with dual AC/DC output, which means they can power virtually any type of device without additional hardware.

Solar input

The maximum wattage figure in a generator's specs represents the maximum electricity it can process from connected solar panels. Some generators feature a Maximum Power Point Tracking (MPPT) charge controller, which optimizes charging efficiency by finding the ideal operating current and voltage for current conditions. MPPT controllers meaningfully improve both capacity utilization and long-term battery health.

Interface and compatibility

Control panel complexity and available connection types vary widely. Some models offer standard wall outlets and little else; others include USB-C, USB-A, and Bluetooth connectivity for mobile app monitoring and control. Wireless capability is particularly convenient for generators used as home backup systems, since it allows you to check status and adjust settings without physically accessing the unit.

Portability

For generators used for camping, outdoor events, or other recreational activities, portability is a real differentiator. Beyond weight, consider wheel size and build quality. Larger, more durable wheels make a meaningful difference when rolling a heavy unit across uneven ground or loading it into a vehicle.

Expandability

Many solar generators support modular expansion by connecting additional battery packs, linking multiple units, or adding solar panel inputs. If your budget doesn't yet reach your ideal setup, buying a model that supports future expansion lets you upgrade over time without starting from scratch.

Buying guide: how to choose the best solar portable generator

There is no one-size-fits-all answer. The right generator will depend on your energy needs, intended use, and budget. Here's a step-by-step framework.

1. Determine your budget

Your budget is your primary constraint. Generally, higher capacity and more advanced technology mean a higher generator cost. Get a realistic sense of what you can comfortably spend, but keep in mind that buying slightly more capacity now is almost always cheaper than replacing an undersized unit later.

2. Figure out your power needs

Whether you're planning recreational use or home backup, you'll need to calculate how much power you actually need. List every device or appliance you want to run, note its wattage draw, and consider whether they'll run simultaneously. If your budget rules out a generator with enough total capacity, prioritize your most essential needs and size to those first.

3. Match your inverter specs

Ensure your chosen generator has a pure sine wave inverter with dual AC/DC capability. This combination lets you safely power sensitive electronics and run the widest possible range of devices. Modified sine wave inverters are significantly riskier for electronics and should generally be avoided.

4. Weigh size vs. portability

Consider whether you'll be moving your generator frequently to campsites or events, or whether it will mostly sit in one place as a home backup. For frequent transport, lighter units with quality wheels are worth prioritizing. For stationary home use, the added weight of higher-capacity models is far less of a factor.

5. Compare solar charging speeds

Input wattage determines how fast your generator recharges via solar panels. This matters more for recreational users and for homes in northern regions with limited winter daylight. Check manufacturer specs for estimated full-charge time at maximum solar input, and compare those figures across models before buying.

6. Consider future expansion

Modular solar generator systems let you grow your setup over time. If your ideal configuration is currently out of budget, buying a unit that supports battery expansion or additional panel connections allows you to upgrade as your situation changes, without starting from scratch.

Maintenance tips for solar generators

Solar portable generators don't require nearly as much regular maintenance as gas-powered units, but they do need some ongoing care. Key maintenance tasks include:

Keeping solar panels clean and angled correctly for maximum sun exposure
Storing lithium-ion batteries at moderate temperatures — extreme cold or heat degrades capacity
Monitoring MPPT charge controllers periodically for efficiency anomalies
Testing system functionality, output accuracy, and safety features on a regular schedule
Bottom line: which solar generator is for you?

Any of the five models on this list represents a strong choice, but the right one depends on your specific situation. The EcoFlow DELTA Pro 3 is the best overall option for serious home backup and extended off-grid use. The Goal Zero Yeti PRO 4000 is the pick for disaster preparedness and demanding outdoor work sites. The Anker SOLIX F3800 is ideal for RV owners and anyone needing 240-volt appliance support. The Bluetti AC200L hits the sweet spot for mid-size portability, and the Jackery Explorer 2000 Plus is the most accessible entry point into a modular solar setup on a tighter budget.

Carefully consider how you plan to use your generator, what you need it to power, and what your realistic budget allows. Then use the specs and comparisons in this guide to match those needs to the right model.

 Skip to content Best Portable Power Stations of 2026
 Quick answer: The Jackery Explorer 2000 v2 is our top pick for most buyers — a 2,042Wh LiFePO4 station with a 2,200W continuous output, a 1.75-hour full AC charge, and the most established warranty/support network of any brand in this list. If you want faster solar recharging, the EcoFlow DELTA 2 Max takes a 1,000W solar array to 80% in under an hour. If price-per-watt-hour is your priority, the Anker SOLIX C2000 Gen 2 matches the Jackery’s core specs at a lower typical price. The newest entry, the Anker SOLIX S2000 (launched mid-2026), regularly sells for roughly $600-650 despite a $1,199 list price, making it the best deal of the group right now if you don’t need the absolute highest continuous output.
 We compared five current 1,100-2,100Wh-class portable power stations from the four brands with the strongest track record in this category — Jackery, EcoFlow, Bluetti, and Anker SOLIX — on the specs that actually affect how a station performs during a power outage, a camping trip, or a day of remote work: usable capacity, continuous and surge output, charge speed, and solar input.

 Comparison at a Glance

 EcoFlow DELTA 2 Max 2,048Wh 2,400W (3,400W X-Boost) 1.1 hrs (80%) 1,000W 50.7 lbs ~$1,199

 Jackery Explorer 2000 v2 — Best Overall
 The Explorer 2000 v2 pairs a 2,042Wh LiFePO4 battery with a 2,200W continuous / 4,400W surge inverter, which is enough headroom to start most single motor-driven appliances (a mini fridge, a sump pump) without tripping. Jackery rates the battery for roughly 4,000 cycles to 70%+ capacity and backs it with a 3-year standard warranty (extendable to 5 years by registering on Jackery’s site). A full AC recharge takes about 1.75 hours, or as fast as 1.7 hours in the emergency-charge mode.
 Best for: buyers who want the most established brand support network and a solid all-around balance of capacity, output, and charge speed.
 Skip if: you specifically need the fastest possible solar recharging — its 400W max solar input is the lowest of the four here.
 Read our full Jackery Explorer 2000 v2 review for the complete spec breakdown and who it’s best for.
 Check current price at Jackery.com → or on Amazon → 
 EcoFlow DELTA 2 Max — Fastest Solar Recharging
 The DELTA 2 Max accepts up to 1,000W of solar input across dual MPPT trackers rated over 99% efficiency — combined with AC input, EcoFlow claims an 80% charge in as little as 43 minutes. Its 2,400W continuous output with X-Boost technology can push appliances up to 3,400W by briefly borrowing headroom from the inverter’s safety margin. EcoFlow backs it with a 5-year warranty, the longest of this group, and the unit is expandable to 6kWh with add-on batteries.
 Best for: off-grid or frequent-outage use where fast solar recharging matters more than raw price.
 Skip if: weight matters — at 50.7 lbs it’s the heaviest station in this comparison.
 Read our full EcoFlow DELTA 2 Max review for the complete spec breakdown and who it’s best for.
 Check current price on Amazon → 
 Anker SOLIX C2000 Gen 2 — Best Value
 The C2000 Gen 2 matches the DELTA 2 Max’s 2,048Wh capacity and 2,400W output, with a slightly higher 4,000W surge rating, while typically retailing well below both the Jackery and EcoFlow. Anker rates the LFP battery for 4,000 cycles to 80% capacity — the highest cycle-life claim of the four — and a full charge takes about 88 minutes on AC alone, or as fast as 45 minutes combining AC and solar.
 Best for: buyers who want 2,000Wh-class specs without paying flagship pricing.
 Skip if: you want the absolute longest brand track record — Anker’s SOLIX energy line is newer to the power-station category than Jackery or EcoFlow.
 Read our full Anker SOLIX C2000 Gen 2 review for the complete spec breakdown and who it’s best for.
 Check current price on Amazon → 
 Bluetti AC180 — Best Compact Option
 The AC180 trades capacity for portability — at 1,152Wh and 35.3 lbs, it’s noticeably smaller and lighter than the other three, while still delivering 1,800W continuous output (2,700W surge in Power Lifting Mode), enough for most single large appliances. It supports pass-through charging and is compatible with Bluetti’s B80/B230/B300 expansion batteries if you need more capacity later. Bluetti backs it with a 5-year warranty and rates the battery for 3,500+ cycles to 80% capacity.
 Best for: buyers who want a lighter, more portable unit and are willing to trade some capacity for it, with the option to expand later.
 Skip if: you need 2,000Wh+ of capacity out of the box — the AC180 tops out around half that.
 Read our full Bluetti AC180 review for the complete spec breakdown and who it’s best for.
 Check current price on Amazon → 
 Anker SOLIX S2000 — Newest Launch, Best Deal Right Now
 Launched in mid-2026, the SOLIX S2000 pairs a 2,010Wh LiFePO4 battery with a 1,500W continuous / 3,000W peak inverter — a lower continuous rating than the other three, but enough for a full-size fridge, most lighting circuits, and small appliances during an outage. Anker rates the battery for 10,000 cycles and a roughly 15-year design life, well above the 3,500-4,000 cycle claims of the other three, and a full AC charge takes about 1.7 hours (1.2 hours to 80%). The list price is $1,199.99, but it has sold consistently around $599-649 since launch, which makes it the best price-per-Wh in this comparison whenever that discount is active.
 Best for: buyers prioritizing price and long cycle life over maximum continuous wattage.
 Skip if: you need to run higher-draw appliances simultaneously — its 1,500W continuous output is the lowest of the five stations here.
 We haven’t published a full standalone review of the S2000 yet — this comparison reflects manufacturer specifications and third-party reviews, not our own hands-on testing.
 Check current price on Amazon → 
 How We Chose
 This comparison is based on manufacturer-published specifications and publicly available data, not hands-on testing — we have not physically tested every unit listed here. We selected these four models because they represent the current mainstream 1,100-2,100Wh tier from the four brands with the strongest US market presence and support networks, and we prioritized specs that affect real-world outage and off-grid performance: continuous/surge output, charge speed, solar input, and warranty coverage. The Anker SOLIX S2000 was added in August 2026 to reflect its mid-2026 launch and its consistent discounted pricing since then. We did not accept payment from any manufacturer to be included in this comparison; some links above are affiliate links, and we may earn a commission if you buy through them at no extra cost to you — see our Affiliate Disclosure for details.
 Frequently Asked Questions
 Which of these can run a full-size refrigerator? All four can start and run a typical residential fridge (100-800W running, 1,000-2,200W starting) — the Bluetti AC180’s lower 2,700W surge is the tightest fit if your fridge has a high starting surge.
 Do I need the 2,000Wh+ tier, or would a smaller station work? If you’re mainly charging phones, laptops, and running lights, a sub-$500 station is usually enough — see our battery size calculator to check your actual Wh need before spending more than necessary.
 Is LiFePO4 better than the older NMC batteries these brands used to sell? Yes, for this use case — LiFePO4 rates for roughly 2-4x more charge cycles and is significantly more thermally stable. All four models here use LiFePO4.
 Can I add solar panels to any of these later even if I don’t buy them now? Yes — all four accept third-party solar panels within their rated voltage/wattage range, not just the manufacturer’s own panels, as long as the connector matches or you use an adapter.

 Whether you are outfitting your home in case of an extended power outage or looking for a steady supply of off-grid power for your overlanding setup, it’s never been a better time to purchase a solar generator. But sifting through all the available options on the market — power stations that are lunchbox-sized to luggage-sized, solar panels that can pack in a backpack to multiple eight-foot long panels you chain together — can take a lot of time and effort. To help you choose the best solar generator for your purpose, we tested some of the most innovative models from Jackery, EcoFlow, Goal Zero, Bluetti, Anker, BioLite, Lion Energy, Ugreen, Vtoman, and more to see how they stacked up.

 How I Tested the Best Solar Generators
 There are two components to a solar generator: a solar panel and a power station. In my first and second rounds of testing of solar generators — in 2022 and 2023 — I focused on tandem testing to see how much power each pairing could produce, side-by-side, in the field. 
 An early test I ran of the best solar generators. Laura Lancaster 
 While this testing was valuable for learning about solar generators, and the issues that can arise out in the field, it didn’t provide sufficient granular information about the performance differences between the sola -generator components. So for my third round of testing I separated out the power stations and the solar panels and put them each through a series of rigorous tests. 
 Testing the Solar Panels
 One of many rounds or solar panel testing I conducted over the last two years. Laura Lancaster 
 In a solar generator setup, solar panels are what generate power. To determine how effective they were at doing just that, I tested 14 different solar panels both under clear skies and under clouds. This testing was conducted over the course of several years, with the same Anker SOLIX 100W panel serving as the control for each test. 
 ↓ Jump to Testing Results for Recommended Solar Panels 
 I also evaluated the panels on their portability and ease of use. Finally, I looked at their lowest operating temperature and their IP rating — a third-party test of water resistance and dust resistance. 
 Read the Full Story: The Best Portable Solar Panels 
 Testing the Power Stations
 Testing the max wattage potential of the power station component of the best solar generators. Laura Lancaster 
 If the solar panels are what is generating your power, the power station is what captures it, stores it, and releases the power when you need it. But the power station also uses some of that stored energy to power itself. I tested 9 power stations with the latest LiFePo4 battery chemistry on both a low draw (34 watts) and a high draw (380 watts) to see which was the most efficient at converting stored power to usable power. I also evaluated portability and ease of use. For this test, I started from scratch, calling in units from nine different manufacturers for testing in February 2024. Between June and September 2024, I additionally conducted long-term storage testing, to validate how much capacity users can expect to lose over time. 
 ↓ Jump to Testing Results for Recommended Power Stations 
 I also considered the maximum solar input of each power station as well as its lowest operating temperature and IP rating. 
 Read the Full Story: The Best Portable Power Stations 
 Choosing a Solar Generator Package
 While it is possible to mix and match solar panels and power stations, it can be a bit tricky. You need to make sure that the ports are compatible, as different brands use different connectors. You also need to make sure that the power station can handle the power input of the solar panel. For this story, I chose solar generators where the power station and solar panel components were made by the same company. 
 How I’m Assessing Price and Value
 As of 2025, I’m evaluating solar generator packages on their price and relative value. The challenge with this analysis is that, in this category, “list price” is essentially meaningless. More often than not, solar generator manufacturers will run so-called sales on their products, to create the illusion that you are getting an especially great deal if you jump now to pick up a unit. Sometimes, especially around Black Friday, this is true. Usually it’s not. It’s companies trying to manufacture the false impression among consumers that something is a “deal” so that they make an uninformed purchase. Don’t fall for it, especially not in a category that’s this pricey. 
 In the below table, I’m assessing price in a few different ways. My primary tool for this is the Keepa widget. 
 High Price: The highest price across the last 180 days 
 Low Price: The lowest price across the last 180 days
 Solar generators are packages composed of two products: power stations and solar panels. Some solar generators emphasize the power station portion of the setup, while others emphasize the solar panel portion. To estimate expected costs for each package, I first considered the expected price per watt hour (Wh). I determined this by looking at the average cost per usable watt hour from the units in the 1,000 Wh range in my test of the best portable power stations . This was $0.82 per watt hour. Next, I looked at the average cost per produced watt from the claimed 200W options in my test of the best portable solar panels. This was $2.84 per produced watt. 
 I then use these two numbers to estimate the value of each package using the known usable watt hours and the known produced watts for each piece of the product. In the below table, I also have the high and low price over the last 180 days, from the Keepa widget. Finally, I compare the actual value of each solar generator (using my formula) to the low price and the highest price to give you a sense of how much you could potentially save (or be overcharged). Keep in mind that the max potential savings will likely only be available during special shopping events, like Black Friday or Amazon Prime Day.

 Jackery’s power stations have always stood out to me as being exceptionally easy to use, sort of like the iPhone of portable power stations. Their display panel is straightforward and intuitive, their bright-orange charging cables are color-coded to the power station itself. Anker and EcoFlow also do a great job in this area, but not quite at the level of Jackery. If you only expect to break out your power station once or twice a year, being able to quickly reorient yourself to how to use the unit is important. 
 Also: Jackery Explorer 1000 Plus bundle available
 The Explorer 2000 Plus has an output of 3000 watts, which is enough juice to power many modern refrigerators. Its battery life of 2043 watt-hours means it can supply that power for about a day before needing to be powered up again via a solar panel setup. During my testing of the Explorer 1000 Plus model, it proved to be about middle of the road for efficiency, providing more usable power for higher-wattage appliances on average. Because of a durability issue (a crack in the housing), I am not recommending this unit for individuals who expect to use their power station on the regular. 
 I originally tested the SolarSaga 200W solar panel as a full setup, with four panels plugged into a single power station. This test showed the full power of the array, which registered 650 watts of power generation on a sunny (albeit hazy) day. I recently retested a single panel in tandem with the rest of the units in this review, and under completely clear skies, the panel was even more impressive: It registered 184 watts of energy coming from a single panel. It was also a standout performer in cloudy weather, producing 49 watts of power. It’s also the only panel I’ve seen pull power out of low-light conditions (covered patio at dusk). I still haven’t found another solar panel of this size that performs at this level. It’s one of my top picks. 
 The Jackery SolarSaga 200W is powerful and easy to use solar panel. 
 Like with the power station, Jackery makes this one exceptionally easy to use, with color-coded cables and connectors that you can use to pair additional panels with the power station. 
 Each of the panels has three kickstands, which provided plenty of stability during testing. Laura Lancaster

 The EcoFlow Delta 2 stood out from the competition in my testing of the best portable power stations for its overall efficiency in turning stored power into usable power as well as its low weight and easy-to-use interface. This backs up my impression of the Delta 2 Max, which has the same battery chemistry and design, just more watt-hour capacity. If you want a power station for a solar generator setup, it’s hard to do better than this. 
 The Jackery Explorer 2000 Plus sits next to the similarly powerful EcoFlow Delta Max 2. Laura Lancaster 
 Something different about the EcoFlow Delta 2 Max compared to other power stations I’ve looked at is that the six AC outlets (as well as the car outlet) are on the back side of the power station, with the solar and AC input ports. This can be a bit of a chore if you plan to swap out cords on a regular basis, but if you’re setting up a static off-grid system that you won’t be fiddling with too much, it has a nicer aesthetic.

 While this power station, like others in my test, does come with an app, I don’t recommend using it as these have a significant power draw on the units. 
 It’s hard to find a better value than the EcoFlow 220W Bifacial Portable Solar Panel. It produces more power for its cost and weight than anything else I’ve tested. And its XT-60 connector cable means it’s compatible out of the box with other power stations, including the Anker SOLIX F2000.
 Also: EcoFlow Delta 2 bundle available
 The downside to this solar panel is that it is surprisingly difficult to set up, and pretty fiddly to adjust. It will also warp if left in storage long-term. While the other solar panels in this test rely on adjustable kickstand legs to optimize the angle of the panel toward the sun, the EcoFlow 220W Bifacial Portable Solar Panel takes a different approach: It uses the carrying case to support the panel. First, four clips attach to the four corners of the carrying case. You then clip into the panel itself, angling the carrying case at a wedge to create structure to the panel. The angle of the panel can be adjusted by zipping the carrying case up or down. 
 While I appreciate that the carrying case is serving multiple functions with the EcoFlow 220W Bifacial Portable Solar Panel, the actual setup can be a little time-consuming. 
 As you can see, this does work. I was able to set up the panel to face the sun at an optimal angle, but I found that zippering up the carrying case to adjust the angle of the panel once it was already in position was fairly difficult. I wouldn’t want to take down and set up the EcoFlow 220W Bifacial Portable Solar Panel on a regular basis, but I’m happy to do it once given its performance potential.

While the Jackery’s telescoping handle never extended far enough to allow me to stand upright, it was comfortable to pull the Anker SOLIX F2000 by its handle for short distances. This included over very muddy ground during one of my early tests in the summer of 2023. If you regularly move your power stations more than 50 feet at a time, then the ease and comfort with which you can maneuver the Anker SOLIX F2000 makes it a smart choice.
 After testing, I can confirm that the wheels on the Anker 767 PowerHouse are more than capable of handling a variety of rugged terrains. Laura Lancaster 
 In my test of the best portable power stations, the Anker SOLIX C1000, which uses the same battery chemistry as this model, was a top performer. It was very efficient at delivering large and small amounts of power. Unlike the C1000 model, the Anker Solix F2000 comes with an RV plug built in and a max wattage of 2400 watts (which I did test), equivalent to what a typical RV uses in a day.
 Trying to make a dent in the Anker SOLIX F2000’s output capacity. Laura Lancaster 
 The Anker SOLIX 200W Solar Panel was the simplest to use of the larger solar panels I looked at. I liked that it didn’t have a separate carrying case to mess with, and a simple carabiner and mesh bag combo did the trick to stash the relevant cable and ensure it didn’t become separated from the larger unit. Like all of these kickstand solar panel setups, it was a little cumbersome to use, but extra reinforcement on the three kickstand legs were useful, to an extent, when adjusting the panel to a lower angle.
 A mesh bag was a simple solution that kept the cord with the solar generator when not in use. Laura Lancaster 
 While this solar panel isn’t quite as powerful as the Jackery SolarSaga 200W, it easily produced over 75 percent of its 200-watt capability during my tests — and the Anker SOLIX F2000 can support up to five of these chained together. Strangely, this panel does not have the same sundial component that the Anker SOLIX 100W does. However, after I set up the Anker SOLIX 100W, I adjusted the Anker SOLIX 200W panel to match its angle and immediately saw a 23-watt difference in the power input. Hopefully, Anker will simply add this accessory onto the 200W model in the future, but in the meantime, you can purchase a clip-on sundial separately.

 Something you see over and over when you’re looking at the fine print on power stations are reminders to protect them from the elements. Rain, dirt, and dust can wreak havoc on the ports and inner workings of these devices. For those of us that love the outdoors and plan to use these devices camping or overlanding, this is a bit of a conundrum.
 The Bluetti AC60 is one of the only power stations I’ve tested that is rated to fully protect against dust and “water jets,” i.e., rain. (Note that it’s not water resistant to the point that you can drop it in a lake.) 
 I tested the Bluetti AC180 as part of my test of the best portable power stations. While I wasn’t overly impressed with that unit’s performance relative to others on the market, it fared well enough, such that the AC60s unusual weather-resistant bonafides pushed it over the line into my top camping pick. 
 The Bluetti PV120 Solar Panel is one of the best solar panels I’ve tested. Despite being a similar size and price compared to the Anker SOLIX 100W (a 100-watt solar panel), it produced 16 more watts during testing.

 Its kickstands had snap buttons at the adjustment points, making it simpler to find the correct angle than on solar panels that liked that feature. It also has snaps that hold the package together when folded up, eliminating the need for an extra carrying case. This has become my new go-to panel when I head out camping.

 Whether you are living in a small apartment or a crowded house, there isn’t always a lot of space to stash gear that you aren’t using daily, including emergency gear. Despite the petite size of the Anker SOLIX C1000, it’s a surprisingly powerful power station. It can handle a hearty solar input load, up to 600 watts. It can also put out 2400 watts at 120 volts, which will allow you to power most anything, from a fridge, to a CPAP machine, to a microwave.
 Testing the Anker SOLIX C1000 Solar Generator against a similarly sized setup from Lion Energy. Laura Lancaster 
 While Anker is boasting that this has an extremely fast turnover in the event of a power outage, which would theoretically allow you to keep critical systems going without a hitch, the reality is that the power it holds (1056Wh) and can generate at a time (200 watts) may not be enough to sustain you for a longer power outage. If there is medical equipment that is necessary for your or your loved’s one day-to-day survival, look into a larger power station with more solar input potential like the Anker SOLIX F2000. But if you’re looking for a unit that can keep everyone’s phones juiced with the option to turn on your coffee maker, then this one is hard to beat. 
 I had previously recommended pairing the Anker SOLIX C1000 with Anker’s 100-watt solar panel; however, they have made some changes to this model since I last tested it. The most noticeable change was the removal of the sundial feature, which is essential, in my experience, for maximizing the power output of a smaller unit. As such, I’m now recommending their larger 200W solar panel, described above in the recommendation for the best solar generator for RVs. While Anker’s 200W panel is more cumbersome than I would prefer, it will still provide plenty of power even when not optimally pointed toward the sun. Critically, even someone of a smaller stature can carry both the panel and the power station at the same time. If you’re interested in checking out the older model of the Anker SOLIX 100W, you can purchase a refurbished version of it on Amazon .

 In recent years, power station technology has advanced to Lithium Iron Phosphate (LiFePo4) , overtaking other lithium formulations, including lithium ion and NCM, for its longevity potential. These new formulations will last up to four times as long as older portable power stations. As such, I have removed power stations from the list that do not use this technology, including older models from Jackery and Anker, as well as the Goal Zero Yeti 1500X and the BioLite BaseCharge. I especially recommend avoiding power stations that utilize NCM chemistry, as one of the key components, cobalt, is associated with significant human rights atrocities in the Congo . 
 While I was tempted to include Goal Zero’s excellent weather-resistant Yeti 700X on this list, their solar panels are lacking. The Boulder panels, while cost effective, do not generate enough power relative to their size. The Nomad series does better, but neither the 100W panel nor the 200W panel have a handle on the carrying case. 
 While I was initially impressed with Lion Energy’s package of their Summit power station along with one of their 100-watt solar panels , further testing of the power station revealed that it is not effective at storing power long term. 
 I have also tested power stations and solar panels from Vtoman, Ugreen, and Dakota Lithium. Unfortunately, at this point, I have not found their performance to be on par with others in this category. See more in the results section for the best portable power stations and the best portable solar panels . 
 I tested the Zendure SuperBase V6400 paired with their 400W Solar Panel as part of my spring testing. This unit is massive: It comes saran-wrapped up on a pallet. While it does have wheels and a handle, that does not make it portable. It took a merciful delivery driver and myself an hour to get it up three floors to my home. This is not a realistic choice for overlanders or campers. Unless your rig has a ramp and a ton of excess of space I wouldn’t even consider it. Picture a 45 liter Yeti Tundra cooler that weighs 130 pounds.
 There were also problems with the Zendure SuperBase V6400 itself. The unit I had did not have functioning USB-C ports. I also noted that simply leaving the AC ports on overnight resulted in a 10 percent drop in the unit’s overall battery; surprising, given how many watt-hours it holds. Zendure confirmed that this is the expected functioning of the unit. One aesthetic note is that the latches for some of the port covers did not close correctly. The Zendure 400W Solar Panel was another story: It was surprisingly lightweight and easy to use given how much juice it generated. I only wish I could have paired it with a different power station.
 I strongly recommend heavily researching this unit before making a purchase, as you may be stuck with it. It requires original shipping materials (which I no longer had) and a pallet to return it. Local shipping companies were unable to supply one (at one point, Zendure suggested I purchase a pallet). I was unable to return this unit and it ultimately found its way to an acquaintance who works in IT. They’ve rigged it up to be the sole source of power for their bedroom, including servers and computers. They’re considering trying to use it as a source of power for their Tesla. If that sounds like what you’re hoping to do with your solar generator, then by all means give the Zendure package a look, but if you’re primarily looking for a unit for backup emergency power or for outdoors use, I’d give this one a pass.

 What Size Solar Generator Do I Need?
 If you’re looking to purchase a solar generator for the first time, the number of specifications to consider can be overwhelming. How many watt hours do you need? What is the difference between volts and amps? What’s a watt surge, anyway? Unless you’re already an electrician, it can be a steep learning curve.
 To help find a simpler answer to the question of what size solar generator you need for your home, I spoke to Ben Pattison, Director of Product Development at Goal Zero. As it turns out, the first thing that consumers should look for starts at home: “The primary question for someone to think about is what matters, what’s critical, and how long do I want to run it for,” said Pattison. “That’s really what’s gonna guide the decision-making for them.”
 Unfortunately, there isn’t a quick and easy way to estimate your energy needs. While it is theoretically possible to look at the meter for your house, most people only run critical systems during an emergency. And “critical” tends to be a pretty subjective term. For some people it could be their refrigerator and their space heater. For others, it could be a TV or other entertainment system. For instance, if you wanted to be able to run your refrigerator for a day (uses 67 watts per hour) and fully charge your lap top once per day (typically 51Wh), you’d need a power station that could had at least 1,659 watt-hour capacity. 
 You’ll also need to see what the maximum draw is for each of your electronics. While a refrigerator may use an average of 67 watts per hour, it doesn’t use that energy evenly: sometimes it will use 6 watts, sometimes it will surge and need 800 watts. Typically you can determine this number by multiplying the watt requirements by six (to guesstimate the needs), or by multiplying the amps and volts ratings together.
 At 115 volts, I can use three out of the five of the power stations in my test to power my fridge. Laura Lancaster 
 So the power station size you need will in large part depend on what your definition of “critical” is, with some individuals content to rough it as long as they can keep their phone charged and the space heater running while others may want something more substantial. For the former group, a best-in-class power station often suffices, as you can simply pick it up and move it to whichever room you currently need power in. But if you plan to power a larger chunk of your home, that quickly leads to a mess of power stations and extension cords. 
 Fortunately, Goal Zero is one of the solar generator companies that also sells solutions akin to gas generators. Their Haven 10 manual transfer switch gives you the option to back up 10 circuits in your home, transferring them over to power for your solar generator at the flip of a switch. However, this will (for most people) involve calling an electrician out to get it installed.
 While there are times when you know exactly when a blackout is going to happen and how long it’s going to last for (such as if your electrical utility is planning a rolling blackout), oftentimes people have no idea when a blackout is going to occur. That can make estimating your power needs as much art as science — during testing I saw the AC output regularly jump between 250 watts to over 1,000 watts depending on what appliances I was running. It’s also tough to know exactly how much you’ll be using each appliance in a power outage event — will you need to power a space heater during winter, or an air conditioner in the summer months?
 “That’s where solar becomes really important,” says Pattison. “Unfortunately, the sun isn’t consistent.” He suggests that people use the “rule of five” when determining how much solar they will need for their solar generator. For instance, if you’re purchasing a 4,000 watt hour power station, you’ll need 800 watts of solar to charge it up during the day. If it’s a 2,000 watt hour power station, you’ll need 400 watts of solar. However, if you know that the sun is even more limited at critical times of the year where you live, take that into consideration before making a final purchase. 
 Other Things to Consider Before Choosing the Best Solar Generator
 Budget
 Solar generators can be a pricey investment. Before you start looking at the various power stations and solar panels and package deals available, it’s important to know how much you are willing to spend. Underspending on a power station can result in inadequate power needs in the case of a power outage or while adventuring off grid. 
 Portability
 Power stations are often heavy, and solar panels can be unwieldy. Purchasing a larger unit than is necessary for your needs can reduce the utility of your overall setup — after all, if you hesitate to pull out your solar generator because of what a pain it is to set up, then it’s not doing you much good after all.
 Size
 While a single power station or a single solar panel may not take up much space, combined, they can start to add up. Consider how much storage space you have before making a final purchase. 
 FAQs
 Q: Are solar-powered generators worth the money? Solar-powered generators are expensive, especially if you are looking to power high-energy appliances, but for many people the peace of mind they bring makes them more than worth the money. Also, compared to gas-powered generators, solar-powered generators are quieter, lighter, and are free to recharge (no fuel costs), and so for many people are less expensive over the long run. The key is making sure you select a unit that can hold and generate enough power to run whatever you plan to plug in for an extended amount of time.
 Q: How do I choose a portable solar generator? While estimating your energy needs during a surprise blackout can be tough, if you are shopping for a solar generator for a car camping, RV, or overlanding setup, then you’ll be able to hone in more closely on your exact requirements. That’s because the manufacturers for these products assume that most individuals will be using them off the grid, and can provide reasonable estimates of how much juice you’ll need to power them for a set amount of time. 
 Q: Can a solar generator run a refrigerator? Yes, some solar generators can run refrigerators. There are two numbers that you need to line up when choosing the right solar generator for your needs: volts and watt-hours. First, look to see what the voltage requirements are of your refrigerator — you can typically find this on a sticker on the inside of your fridge.
Then choose a power station that can meet the voltage needs of your refrigerator. The watt-hours (Wh) essentially represent the size of the battery in your power station — the larger the battery, the longer it will power your fridge for, and the more it will cost. Typically, a 2,000Wh power station has enough juice to run your fridge for a day, but that depends on the power needs of your refrigerator, including the ambient air temperature and any add-ons running in the background. If you expect to have a solar generator powering a refrigerator for an extended period of time, choose larger, more powerful solar panels to pair with it, so that your refrigerator spends less time unplugged while the power station is recharging. 
 Q: Can a solar generator run an air conditioner? Yes, a solar generator paired with a power station can run an air conditioner. One thing you have to keep in mind is that the air conditioner’s power needs must match the power output of your power station. 
 Final Thoughts on the Best Solar Generators
 After testing the best solar generators for over a year — both individually and in tandem — it’s clear that the Jackery Solar Generator 1000 Pro (or 2000 Pro, depending on your power station needs) is one of the best setups available. While the Jackery combo can often be had on sale, if you’re looking to spend less money overall, the EcoFlow Delta 2 Max is a great option if you’re comfortable with a slightly more complicated setup. If you have a strong idea of exactly what your energy needs are, check out the sheer number of options offered by Goal Zero — panels that vary from 100W to 300W and power stations that go up to 6,000 watt-hours. Individuals and families on the go will appreciate the portability of the BioLite duo, while overlanders will benefit from the juice and portability of the Anker SOLIX F2000 power station and 531 Solar Panel.

 A portable power station is a battery, an inverter and a charger in one box, and the box's spec sheet is now written to be misread. Surge watts pose as continuous output, capacities are quoted for expansion configurations the base unit does not contain, and cycle-life figures silently change their endpoint — 4,000 cycles to 80% capacity and 4,000 cycles to 70% are different products wearing the same number. This ranking reads the makers' own documents instead: per-model manuals and spec sheets for chemistry and cycle life, published warranty and support terms for accountability, and each product's own Amazon aggregate for satisfaction, gathered the same way for all twenty-three candidates.
 We screened twenty-three current US models and ranked ten, all of them LiFePO4, all priced on the station alone at a verified street price — the maker's own US store or Amazon, checked in late October 2026, never a coupon or bundle figure. The ranking spans 768Wh to 3,600Wh because that is the portable premise: below it, a station cannot carry a refrigerator through an outage night; above it — the 240V whole-home class — the box stops being portable in any honest sense, and those units are named in the cut list rather than ranked. Gas generators, inverter-only units with no battery, and bare batteries are out of scope entirely.

The field's lesson is that the fight has moved to the fine print: cycle-life endpoints (80% versus 70% versus a 6,500-cycle headline that resolves to 50%), switchover times that differ between a model's manual and its marketing, and fastest-charge figures that quietly assume an app mode or two inputs at once. Read the endpoint before the number.
 Questions, answered
 How much capacity do I actually need?
 Work from the loads, not the marketing. A full-size refrigerator draws 100–200W while its compressor runs and uses roughly 1–1.5kWh per day; lights, phones and a router add a few hundred watt-hours. A 1kWh station (the DELTA 3 Plus, C1000 Gen 2 class) covers a fridge plus essentials for an evening and a night. A 2kWh station covers a full day with margin and is the smallest class that makes sense for a CPAP (about 300–500Wh per night) plus a fridge. The 3,600Wh DELTA Pro is for multi-day outages, well pumps and tool loads. Every ranked unit states its capacity for the base box only — expansion figures are named as expansion, never folded into the headline.
 LiFePO4 or regular lithium-ion — does the chemistry really matter?
 It is the single biggest lifespan divider in this category. Every ranked station uses LiFePO4 (LFP) cells rated for 3,000–4,000 cycles — a decade of regular use. The screened field's lithium-ion NMC units tell the other story: the Goal Zero Yeti 1500X is rated for 500 cycles to 80%, the EcoFlow DELTA Max 2000 for 800, and both were cut on exactly that arithmetic despite strong brands. LFP is also the more thermally stable chemistry. If a station's documents do not name the chemistry, treat that as an answer.
 Why do cycle-life claims range from 500 to 6,500 for similar-looking boxes?
 Because the endpoint moves. The field's honest standard is cycles to 80% of original capacity. Jackery's v2 line and DJI quote their 4,000 cycles to 70% instead — the same count, a more worn-out battery at the end of it — and EcoFlow's DELTA Pro headlines 6,500 cycles, which its own product page clarifies is to 50% capacity (the comparable figure, 3,500 cycles to 80%, is printed on the same page and is what this ranking scores). Compare only like endpoints; this ranking normalizes every claim to its maker's own stated endpoint and scores accordingly.
 Are these prices for the station alone, and why might they differ from what I see today?
 Yes — every ranked price is the station alone, verified on 2026-10-27/28 at the maker's own US store or on Amazon, with no coupon, bundle or panel kit folded in (where a station is sold in solar bundles, the bundle price is recorded separately in the research dossier). This is the most aggressively discounted category in consumer electronics: maker stores run countdown sales and prices rotate weekly, sometimes by hundreds of dollars. The scores use the verified street price at screening, and AmRank's weekly price scan re-checks them after publication — check the current price before buying, because several scores would rise or fall at a different week's figure.
 UPS or EPS — will one of these keep my computer or CPAP running through a switchover?
 Only some. A true UPS-grade switchover is 10 ms or faster: the Anker SOLIX C2000 Gen 2 and C1000 Gen 2 and the EcoFlow DELTA 3 Plus all publish 10 ms or better. EPS-grade units switch in 20–30 ms (the DELTA 2 Max's manual rates 30 ms whatever its marketing says; the RIVER 2 Pro is 30 ms class), which most loads tolerate but sensitive equipment may not — test with your actual device before an outage depends on it. One honest note from the makers themselves: Jackery explicitly advises against relying on its stations for medical or life-support equipment, and that caution is worth generalizing.

 How to choose a solar generator 
 1. Size the battery by watt-hours, not by the word “generator”
 Watt-hours, written as Wh, describe stored energy. They do not guarantee appliance runtime. A practical estimate is:
 Estimated runtime ≈ battery watt-hours × usable-depth factor × efficiency ÷ appliance watts 
 For example, using an illustrative 85% usable-energy factor and 90% conversion efficiency, a 2,048Wh station powering a steady 100W load would be estimated at about 15.7 hours:
 2,048 × 0.85 × 0.90 ÷ 100 ≈ 15.7 hours 
 The 85% and 90% values in that example are planning assumptions, not a measured result for any model. Actual runtime changes with the station’s idle consumption, inverter losses, reserve settings, temperature, battery age, and the appliance’s real draw. A refrigerator rated at a particular wattage may cycle on and off, while a heater may draw close to its full rating continuously.
 Before buying, list the loads you actually need during an outage and calculate them separately. A phone, modem, LED lights, laptop, refrigerator, medical equipment, pump, microwave, and space heater have very different energy profiles.
 2. Check continuous output before surge or peak output
 Continuous AC output is the figure to use when determining whether a station can sustain a load. Surge, peak, or boost output may help with a brief startup demand, but it is not a second continuous rating.
 Refrigerators, freezers, pumps, compressors, power tools, and some heating or kitchen appliances can have startup demands that differ substantially from their running-watt label. Add the continuous wattage of loads that may run at the same time, then check the manufacturer’s startup guidance for motor-driven equipment.
 Do not conclude that a 2,400W power station can continuously run every appliance whose startup surge is below a larger peak number. The station must support both the running load and the startup event, and some products impose additional limits by outlet or operating mode.

 5. Decide whether you need direct plug-in power or home integration
 For basic emergency use, plug selected appliances directly into the power station. This is different from powering household circuits through a wall outlet or improvising a connection to the home’s wiring.

The DELTA Pro 3 and SOLIX F3800 are the most relevant models here for published 120/240V and home-backup capabilities, but neither removes the need to follow the manufacturer’s installation instructions and local electrical requirements.
 For RV use, confirm the station’s output, adapter type, grounding behavior, and the RV’s shore-power requirements. A product marketed as RV-compatible does not mean every adapter, receptacle, or appliance combination is automatically suitable.
 6. Be realistic about portability
 Battery capacity and inverter power add weight quickly. The lightest model here, the DELTA 2 Max, is about 50 pounds. The AC200L and Explorer 2000 Plus are around 62 pounds, while the DELTA Pro 3 and F3800 weigh approximately 113.5 and 132 pounds respectively.
 That makes the categories meaningfully different:

 Occasional two-person moving: AC200L and Explorer 2000 Plus offer more capacity and output but are not light.
 Rolling or semi-permanent backup: DELTA Pro 3 and F3800 are better suited to a garage, utility area, RV setup, or prepared backup location.
 Wheels make a heavy unit easier to reposition; they do not make it easy to lift into a vehicle or carry over stairs.
 Accessories that matter 
 Solar panels and charging cables
 Panels and cables must match the station’s voltage, current, connector, and wiring limits. A generic MC4 cable is not automatically compatible merely because both products use solar connectors.  For a selected model, the most useful accessory search is for model-specific expansion batteries and manufacturer-compatible solar charging equipment. Expansion batteries increase runtime and storage but also add weight, cost, charging complexity, and another component that must be stored and maintained.

 Readers planning home or RV use may need transfer switches, inlets, RV adapters, and compatible charging cables . The exact requirement depends on whether the station will power individual appliances, an RV inlet, selected home circuits, or a 120/240V panel-connected system.

The panel will efficiently convert solar power into electrical energy, which will then be transferred to your solar powered generator, ensuring you have reliable power whenever you need it.

 Storage and environmental protection
 Weather resistance is model-specific. The DELTA Pro 3 has a published IP65 protection rating, but that does not establish equivalent protection for the other units in this list. Keep every station, cable connection, and panel controller within the operating and storage conditions stated by its manufacturer. Avoid assuming that a folding panel, power station, or extension cable is safe to leave exposed to rain simply because it is marketed for outdoor use.
 Solar generators versus gas generators 
 A battery power station has several practical advantages: no combustion exhaust while operating, no fuel storage, no engine oil, and generally simpler plug-in use. It can be recharged from solar panels or the grid and can provide silent or low-noise power depending on the model and load.
 Its limitations are equally important. Battery capacity is finite, high-wattage loads consume it quickly, solar charging slows or stops in poor conditions, and large batteries can be difficult to move. A gas generator can typically be refueled for extended operation, while a solar generator needs access to a charged battery, grid power, or sufficient sunlight.
 “No combustion exhaust” does not mean “impact-free,” and it does not remove the need for ventilation, heat management, dry placement, and electrical safety. Follow the manual for the specific station and connected equipment.
 Which one should you buy? 
 Choose the EcoFlow DELTA Pro 3 if you want the best high-output single-unit option in this group and value 120/240V output, 2,600W solar input, and expansion to 12kWh more than low weight.
 Choose the Anker SOLIX F3800 if your priority is a large home-backup platform with 6,000W output, 120/240V split-phase capability, and a much larger possible battery system.
 Choose the BLUETTI AC200L if you want the strongest overall balance of 2kWh-class capacity, 2,400W output, pure-sine-wave AC, and expansion without moving up to the largest systems.
 Choose the Jackery Explorer 2000 Plus if 1,400W dual-port solar input and a familiar expandable ecosystem matter more than a 0ms UPS claim.
 Choose the EcoFlow DELTA 2 Max if you want a roughly 2kWh station that is substantially easier to move and you can accept its lower solar-input and expansion ceilings.
 Buying checklist 
 Write down the appliances and electronics you need during an outage.
 Calculate their simultaneous running wattage and investigate motor or compressor startup demands.
 Estimate required watt-hours using real duty cycles rather than assuming a refrigerator or pump runs continuously.
 Check continuous output first; treat surge, peak, and X-Boost figures as limited-use specifications.
 Compare solar-input voltage and current limits, not only the headline wattage.
 Confirm whether the battery, panels, cables, adapters, and expansion batteries are included or sold separately.
 Decide whether direct appliance plug-in is enough or whether a qualified electrician must design a transfer-switch or panel-connected installation.
 Measure doors, stairs, vehicle space, and storage locations against the station’s actual weight and dimensions.
 Check warranty terms, regional availability, firmware requirements, and manufacturer support immediately before purchase.
 How these recommendations were evaluated 
 This shortlist uses current official U.S. or manufacturer documentation checked August 12, 2026. It compares published battery capacity, continuous output, surge or boost figures, solar-input limits, expansion options, UPS or emergency-power behavior, weight, warranty information, and intended use.
 No hands-on testing, runtime trials, noise measurements, price tracking, durability testing, or independent safety verification was performed for this guide. Manufacturer claims are therefore presented as rated specifications or capabilities. Prices and bundles were not used for ranking because stable August 2026 street pricing and availability were not established and can vary by country, retailer, and package.
 Frequently Asked Questions 
 Can a solar generator power an entire house?
 Usually not indefinitely, and not automatically. A power station can run selected appliances directly, while whole-home or panel-connected use may require a transfer switch, inlet, compatible home-backup equipment, and professional installation. The DELTA Pro 3 and SOLIX F3800 are the most relevant models here for published 120/240V home-backup capabilities, but their larger system claims describe specific expanded configurations.
 How long will a 2,000Wh solar generator run an appliance?
 There is no single runtime number. A practical estimate is battery Wh multiplied by usable-depth and efficiency factors, divided by the appliance’s actual watts. For example, a 2,048Wh station at an illustrative 85% usable energy and 90% conversion efficiency would support a steady 100W load for about 15.7 hours. Real results vary with idle draw, reserve settings, temperature, battery age, and whether the appliance cycles.
 Are solar generators safe to use indoors?
 These battery systems do not produce combustion exhaust while operating, but “solar generator” is not a universal indoor-safety certification. Follow the specific manufacturer’s requirements for ventilation, heat, moisture, charging, clearances, and connected loads. Never use a portable battery to backfeed household wiring through a standard wall outlet.
 Do I need to buy solar panels separately?
 It depends on the bundle. Verify what is included before ordering. If buying panels separately, match the station’s open-circuit voltage, operating voltage, current limit, connector, and approved series or parallel arrangement. The panel’s advertised wattage is a maximum under favorable conditions, not a guaranteed charging rate.
 Which model is easiest to carry?
 The EcoFlow DELTA 2 Max is the lightest model in this comparison at about 50 pounds. The AC200L and Jackery Explorer 2000 Plus are around 62 pounds, while the DELTA Pro 3 and Anker SOLIX F3800 are approximately 113.5 and 132 pounds. The two largest models are better treated as wheeled or semi-permanent backup systems.
 The Bottom Line 
 The right solar generator is the smallest system that safely meets your actual load, runtime, charging, and installation needs. Pick the DELTA Pro 3 for high-output backup, the SOLIX F3800 for a larger 120/240V platform, the AC200L for balanced 2kWh-class performance, the Explorer 2000 Plus for high solar-input flexibility, or the DELTA 2 Max when portability matters most. Before purchasing, verify current model specifications, included accessories, compatibility, warranty, and local installation requirements.

 A 2,000Wh power station is the size where backup power stops being a phone charger and starts running real appliances. It holds enough energy to keep a full-size refrigerator cold for about a day, run a CPAP for several nights, or power a small RV through an evening of lights, fans and a microwave. It is also the largest size most people can still lift into a car or roll across a garage.
 The class has changed a lot in the past year. See it on Amazon · Buy direct from AFERIY (code THEPOWERSTATION for 2% off).
 Need More Than 2kWh?
 If your outage plan covers a full day of refrigeration, a well pump and a furnace blower, or you run a business from your unit, a single 2kWh battery will be tight.
 Expand a 2kWh unit. The EcoFlow DELTA 3 Max Plus, AFERIY P280, Jackery HomePower 2000 Plus v2 and DJI Power 2000 all reach 10kWh or more with extra batteries. See our expandable power station guide .
 Start bigger. The EcoFlow DELTA Pro 3 holds 4,096Wh and outputs 4,000W, with 240V support for home circuits, per EcoFlow. See it on Amazon . Bluetti has also announced the Apex 200 (2,560Wh, expandable), with a US launch planned for early November.

 How Long Will a 2000Wh Power Station Last?
 Start with usable energy, not the label. Inverter losses mean you get roughly 85% of rated capacity out of the AC outlets, so a 2,048Wh unit delivers about 1,700Wh to AC loads. Divide that by the load in watts to get hours.

 These are estimates. Check the label or a plug-in watt meter for your own appliances, and remember that refrigerators and air conditioners cycle on and off, so their real runtime depends on the room and the weather. Our capacity guide walks through the math in more detail.
 How to Choose a 2000Wh Power Station
 Continuous output. Add up the wattage of everything you want to run at the same time and keep a margin of about 20%. A well pump or air conditioner also needs surge headroom at startup, so check the surge figure for motor loads.
 TT-30 outlet. For an RV, a TT-30R outlet lets you plug the RV's 30A cord straight in. The Anker C2000 Gen 2, AFERIY P280 and Bluetti Elite 200 V2 have one; Anker limits its outlet to 20A.
 Solar input. Higher solar input means a faster refill on a sunny day. 1,000-1,200W can refill a 2kWh battery in about 2-3 hours of strong sun; 800W takes closer to 3-4 hours.
 Expansion. If you might need more than 2kWh later, choose a unit with an expansion battery now. Expansion packs are usually tied to one model or family, so you can't mix brands.
 UPS switchover. For computers, networking gear and medical devices, look for 10 ms or less. Bluetti's 15 ms and EcoFlow DELTA 2 Max's unstated figure are fine for most appliances.
 Weight. Every unit here is 41-54 lbs. If you'll carry it often, the Anker C2000 Gen 2 and Jackery HomePower 2000 Plus v2 are the lightest.
 Warranty and cycle rating. Read the fine print: some warranty years require registration or buying from the maker's store, and cycle ratings use different end points (70% or 80%).
 Frequently Asked Questions
 Can a 2000Wh power station replace a home generator?
 For selected circuits, yes. A 2kWh unit can keep a refrigerator, lights, Wi-Fi, phones and a CPAP running through a typical overnight outage. It can't run central air conditioning, an electric range or a water heater, and it will need recharging (solar, wall power or a generator) to cover multi-day outages. Many households pair a power station for quiet, automatic backup with a generator they run a few hours a day to recharge it. Our power stations vs generators guide compares the two.
 How long until the battery degrades?
 Every unit on this list uses LiFePO4 cells rated for 3,000-6,000 cycles. A cycle is one full discharge; using half the battery counts as half a cycle. At one partial cycle a day, that is many years before the battery reaches its rated end point (70% or 80% of original capacity, depending on the maker). A battery at 80% still works; it just holds less. Lithium cells also age with time, so store the unit at about 50-60% charge when you won't use it for a while, and top it up every few months.
 Can I connect solar panels from a different brand?
 Usually yes, as long as you stay within the power station's input limits. Check two numbers: the maximum input voltage and the maximum input wattage. Measure or calculate your array's open-circuit voltage (panels in series add their voltages) and make sure it stays below the limit, for example 60V on the Jackery HomePower 2000 Plus v2 and the Bluetti Elite 200 V2, or 55V on the AFERIY P280. You may also need an adapter from MC4 to the station's port (XT60, XT90 or Anderson).
 Can I run a 30A RV on a 2000Wh power station?
 You can plug in through a TT-30 outlet, but the power station limits what you can run. At 2,400-2,800W you can run lights, the fridge, the water pump and a microwave in turn, but not the roof air conditioner and the microwave together. A 13,500 BTU RV air conditioner draws well over 1,000W while its compressor runs, so it would drain a 2kWh battery in little more than an hour of compressor time.
 Is 2000Wh enough for a CPAP?
 Yes, with plenty of margin. A CPAP without a heated humidifier draws about 40-60W, so a 2kWh unit covers several nights. Turning off the humidifier and running the CPAP from a DC cable, where the maker offers one, stretches it further. See our CPAP power station guide .
 Conclusion
 For most buyers, the EcoFlow DELTA 3 Max Plus is the most capable 2kWh unit you can buy right now, with the highest output and a 10kWh expansion path. RV owners should look at the Anker SOLIX C2000 Gen 2 for its TT-30 outlet and alternator charging, or the AFERIY P280 for more output, more solar input and a longer warranty at a lower price. If you want one box with nothing to add, the Bluetti Elite 200 V2 has the best like-for-like cycle rating and a TT-30 outlet.
 Whatever you choose, size it to your real loads first: list what must run during an outage, total the watts and the hours, and leave a margin.

The best high-capacity solar generator in 2026 is the EcoFlow DELTA Pro: 3,600Wh, 3,600W of output, 1,600W of solar input and expansion to 25kWh for about $1,799, enough to run a 330W essentials load (fridge, lights, devices, router) for about 9.3 hours. If you do not need that much, the BLUETTI AC200PL (2,304Wh, about $950) costs half as much, the Jackery Explorer 2000 Plus adds 3,000W of output (though on October 12, 2026 Jackery sold it new only in kits from $1,429), and the BLUETTI Apex 300 is the pick if you want a system that scales.

High-capacity units, 2,000Wh and up, do something a 1,024Wh unit cannot: power a refrigerator, lights, device charging and a second major appliance through a night and into the next day.

How we chose: Our picks are based on published specifications, pricing, warranty terms and owner reports. Runtimes are arithmetic from each manufacturer's rated capacity.

How long does a high-capacity solar generator last?

Take a standard home backup load: refrigerator (150W), lighting (60W), device charging (100W) and a router (20W), about 330W in total. Inverters lose about 15%, so runtime (hours) = rated Wh x 0.85 / 330W, with no solar input:

The figures here use planning draws: a conservative 150W average for a full-size fridge (a new ENERGY STAR model averages closer to 63W, so expect longer runtimes).

2,048Wh (DELTA 3 Max, C2000 Gen 2) or 2,042.8Wh (Jackery 2000 Plus): about 5.3 hours
2,304Wh (BLUETTI AC200PL): about 5.9 hours
2,764.8Wh (BLUETTI Apex 300): about 7.1 hours
3,600Wh (DELTA Pro): about 9.3 hours

Add a chest freezer (100W average) and all of those drop by about 23%. Add a 1,500W space heater and you are down to one or two hours. High capacity does not solve every problem, but for essential loads over 8-12 hours you need 3,600Wh or a 2kWh system with solar recharging.

Top tier: EcoFlow DELTA Pro

The DELTA Pro is the unit that defines this category. At 3,600Wh and 3,600W continuous, it runs a well pump on a 120V circuit, a microwave and a fridge together, and most household appliances a mid-size unit cannot. EcoFlow's Smart Home Panel is what makes it real home infrastructure.

On the 330W load, the DELTA Pro delivers about 9.3 hours (3,600 x 0.85 / 330). With 1,600W of panels delivering about 75% of their rating for 4.5 good sun hours, you recover roughly 5,400Wh a day (1,600 x 0.75 x 4.5), more than the battery holds, so on a sunny day it can keep up with a fridge, lights and devices around the clock.

At 99 lb it is not a unit you move often; most owners park it in a utility room or garage. It outputs 120V only; if you need 240V, see the EcoFlow DELTA Pro 3 below. See our EcoFlow DELTA Pro review.

With a full 2,400W array, a clear day yields roughly 8,100Wh (2,400 x 0.75 x 4.5), which covers the base battery plus an expansion battery. For off-grid cabins and homes that want to grow a system over time, it is the most capable path here. See our BLUETTI Apex 300 review.

Also worth a look

Three more units above 3kWh that did not make the main list: the BLUETTI Elite 400 (3,840Wh, 2,600W, trolley wheels, about $1,399 at BLUETTI, or $1,449 as an Amazon pre-order releasing November 2) is the cheapest route to nearly 4kWh; the EcoFlow DELTA 3 Ultra (3,072Wh, 3,600W, TT-30 outlet, about $1,299) is a strong mid-price alternative to the DELTA Pro; and the EcoFlow DELTA Pro 3 (4,096Wh, 4,000W at 120V/240V, about $2,799) is the pick if you need 240V from one unit.

Who should buy in this tier?
Partial home backup

For essential loads through a night and into the next day with solar recharging, the AC200PL covers typical outages economically, and the DELTA Pro handles longer outages and heavier appliances. See our home backup guide.

Full-time RV and off-grid cabin use

Size for your daily load plus a buffer. Many full-time RV setups use 3,000-5,000Wh a day. A single DELTA Pro with 1,600W of solar covers a light RV load; an Apex 300 with an added battery and 2,400W of solar covers a heavier one.

Construction and job-site power

For saws, drills and lights, the Jackery 2000 Plus (3,000W) and DELTA Pro (3,600W) give the most headroom. Units rated 2,400W continuous leave little margin for a circular saw's starting spike. Get 3,000W or more if tools are your main use.

How we chose

We compared manufacturer specifications (capacity, continuous and surge output, solar input, expansion, weight), US pricing in September 2026, warranty terms and owner reports. Runtimes use an 85% efficiency factor applied to rated capacity; real-world results vary with temperature, load mix and state of charge.

For a lower price per watt-hour from a lesser-known brand, the PECRON F3000LFP holds 3,072Wh for about $899, roughly $0.29 per Wh.

Zendure's SuperBase V (6,438Wh semi-solid-state or 4,608Wh LiFePO4, 3,800W) also belongs in this class, though Zendure's US store listed every configuration as unavailable in late September 2026.

Our best solar generators under $2,000 narrows this tier to six picks with a firm price cap, led by the 3,840Wh BLUETTI Elite 400.

Frequently Asked Questions
What is the highest capacity portable solar generator?

Among single-box units, the Jackery Explorer 5000 Plus holds 5,040Wh. The EcoFlow DELTA Pro Ultra's battery holds 6,144Wh but ships as a separate inverter and battery. Expandable systems go much further: the DELTA Pro Ultra to 90kWh and the Jackery 5000 Plus to 60kWh.

How long will a 3,600Wh solar generator last?

On a 330W essentials load (fridge, lights, devices, router), a 3,600Wh unit like the EcoFlow DELTA Pro lasts about 9.3 hours (3,600 x 0.85 / 330). A fridge alone at 150W runs about 20 hours; add a 100W chest freezer and it drops to about 12 hours.

Is the EcoFlow DELTA Pro worth the money?

For homeowners with regular outages of 12 hours or more, it is a strong buy at about $1,899: 3,600Wh, 3,600W, 1,600W of solar input, Smart Home Panel support and expansion to 25kWh. If you need 240V, the DELTA Pro 3 is the better choice.

Can a high-capacity solar generator power a whole house?

Not a whole house at normal use. A 3,600Wh unit covers only a few hours of typical whole-home load. With EcoFlow's Smart Home Panel, the DELTA Pro can back up selected circuits (kitchen, bedroom, medical devices) through a 12-24 hour outage, longer with solar recharging.

What is the difference between the EcoFlow DELTA Pro and DELTA 3 Max?

The DELTA Pro has 3,600Wh (vs 2,048Wh), 3,600W continuous (vs 2,400W), 1,600W solar input (vs 500W), 25kWh expansion and Smart Home Panel support, for about $1,799 vs $899. The DELTA 3 Max weighs 44.8 lb vs 99 lb, so it suits vans and RVs better.

How many solar panels do I need for a 3,600Wh solar generator?

The EcoFlow DELTA Pro accepts up to 1,600W, so four 400W panels hit its limit. EcoFlow quotes about 2.8 hours to full in ideal sun; at a more typical 75% of panel rating, plan on about 3 hours of strong sun (3,600 / 1,200).

Is the BLUETTI Apex 300 better than the EcoFlow DELTA Pro?

They suit different buyers. The DELTA Pro has more base capacity (3,600Wh vs 2,764.8Wh), Smart Home Panel support and expansion to 25kWh. The Apex 300 costs less (about $1,599 vs $1,799), has more solar input (2,400W vs 1,600W), more output (3,840W) and a 6,000-cycle rating, and scales further across linked units.

Can a 2,000Wh solar generator run a sump pump?

Usually, yes. A 1/3 HP sump pump runs at about 800W and can draw roughly 1,300W or more on start. The Jackery Explorer 2000 Plus (3,000W continuous) and Anker SOLIX C2000 Gen 2 (4,000W peak) handle that. Check your pump's label before relying on any unit for flood protection.
